summary:
Nunavut is a territory of Canada and stands under the national human-rights and criminal law framework of the country, supplemented by territorial statute. The Nunavut Human Rights Act prohibits discrimination on the grounds of gender identity and gender expression: members of the Legislative Assembly voted unanimously on third and final reading of Bill 31 on 13 March 2017, and Justice Minister Keith Peterson stated that the amendment would make clear that discrimination against transgender people is prohibited. At the time of that vote Nunavut was the first Canadian territory to list gender identity or expression among the protected grounds in its human-rights law.

Nunavut birth certificates carry a third, non-binary sex designation. On 18 September 2025 members of the Legislative Assembly voted 12-8 in committee of the whole to restore that option through amendments to the Vital Statistics Act, after the standing committee had struck it from Health Minister John Main's May 2025 bill, and the bill was then approved on third reading. Bill sponsor Adam Arreak Lightstone said the Government of Nunavut now joins the rest of Canada in recognising non-binary and transgender individuals.

The territorial government funds transition-related care for transgender and non-binary residents. Reporting of 22 March 2022 records that the Nunavut Health Department began funding such care, with breast augmentation, chest contouring, hysterectomy and vaginoplasty named among the procedures, under a partnership with the Metropolitan Centre of Surgery in Montreal. The local LGBTQ group Positive Space called the funding overdue while flagging information gaps for residents living outside the capital.

No trans-specific violent incident, hate-crime count or victimisation figure for Nunavut itself is documented in this record, and no dated instance of anti-trans violence in the territory appears in it.
tangentialFactors:
National police-reported hate-crime data supplies the only quantified turbulence signal available, and it carries no Nunavut breakdown. Statistics Canada's release 'Police-reported hate crime in Canada, 2024', published 30 March 2026, counts 4,882 police-reported hate crimes, up 1% over the year and 169% since 2018, at a rate of 11.9 per 100,000. Incidents motivated by gender identity or gender expression rose 8% to 139, a fourth consecutive annual increase and a 184% rise since 2020; sexual-orientation-motivated incidents fell 26% to 658, with June 2024 alone recording 113 against a monthly average of roughly 50. The same release reports rates about 2.5 times higher in metropolitan areas than in smaller towns, a distribution that matters for a territory with no metropolitan reporting hub of its own.

Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report, an NGO analysis of police-reported data including gender identity and expression motivations, supplies national 2SLGBTQ+ victimisation context rather than territorial figures.
localsOnly:
Residents of Nunavut may request the non-binary sex designation on a Nunavut birth certificate under the amended Vital Statistics Act as approved on 18 September 2025; the record does not state an effective date for the change or the procedure for applying.

Residents have a territorial statutory route against discrimination: the Nunavut Human Rights Act, as amended in 2017, names gender identity and gender expression among protected grounds in employment, housing and services within territorial responsibility.

Transition-related care is funded for residents through the Nunavut Health Department under the Montreal surgical partnership reported from 22 March 2022. Positive Space flagged at that time that information about the service does not reach residents outside the capital, which remains an access gap for people living in the communities.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Nunavut-specific hate-crime statistics, trans-specific violence counts or survey figures are sourced here; the Statistics Canada and Egale Canada material is national and reports no territorial breakdown, so the territory's own rate is unresolved rather than low.

The record contains no dated account of anti-trans violence in Nunavut, so the most recent documented instance cannot be established from it.

Whether the non-binary birth-certificate amendment took effect, and on what date, is not stated in the sources; the record documents the vote and third-reading approval of 18 September 2025 only.

Whether a visitor or newcomer can access the funded surgical pathway, and on what terms, is not sourced; the reporting describes funding for residents.

National-layer material, including federal hate-crime statistics, Criminal Code amendments and the laws of other provinces, belongs to the parent record and is not restated here.
